"* This passage says that years ago, before big US crises, the writer Jeffrey Eugenides said learning more about your country can make you feel more ashamed, much like learning more about yourself. That idea sits at the center of one of his short stories called Great Experiment in his book Fresh Complaint. The interviewer asks whether people now feel more shame about the nation than about themselves. Eugenides answers that both kinds of shame are about equal. He notes that America’s history includes slavery, which is a deep source of sorrow and reflection. He suggests that if you list faults, you can keep going forever, both for a person and a country. He believes personal issues and national issues are connected. He says that when you deal with current events and meet neighbors, your own past affects how you act. He also says a nation is just people, so its problems are personal too. This is meant to highlight how private feelings and public life create constant tension.

* The scene is a talk with Eugenides at Princeton University, where he has taught for 10 years and is now 57. They are in a new library building that is not finished yet. Someone put a simple paper sign that says “unisex” on the restroom door, showing changing attitudes about gender. This small detail is used to show how campus culture, and perhaps the country, has shifted in the last decade. When he toured with his novel Middlesex after it won a Pulitzer in 2003, he often had to explain what “intersex” meant. Now that term is more familiar, and people are more open to it. The interview tries to make the reader feel welcome in a complex conversation without needing special knowledge. It also hints that public understanding can affect a person’s mental health and sense of belonging. You do not need to know about his girlfriend or private life to get the main point. The main point is that personal identity and national identity shape each other all the time.*"
